steps.title: Add the add function
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, below the comment, write def add(a, b): that returns a + b, then add print(add(2, 3)) at the bottom.

checks.label: add function is written in the

targets.caption: Type the add function on the lines below this comment
Indent the return line by four spaces so it sits inside add

hints: Type the def line right below the comment, then press Enter.
The body of add must be indented under the def line by four spaces.
Leave one blank line, then add print(add(2, 3)) at the bottom and save before running.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the colon after def add(a, b).
Not indenting return a + b, which causes an IndentationError.
Writing add(a, b) with a missing parenthesis or a typo in the name, so the print line fails.
Forgetting to save the file (Ctrl+S / Cmd+S) before running python calculator.py, so the output is stale or missing.
Running the file from a different folder, so Python cannot find calculator.py.

steps.title: Run your first output
steps.instructions: In the terminal, run python calculator.py and check that it prints 5.

checks.label: The add function is still in

precision_checks.label: calculator.py has the print call for

targets.caption: This line is already in your file. It calls add(2, 3) and prints the result. Leave it as is.
In the terminal, type python calculator.py and press Enter.

hints: Make sure the terminal is open in the lesson folder, the same folder that contains calculator.py.
Type the command exactly as python calculator.py (lowercase, with the .py ending) and press Enter.
You should see a single line with 5 under the command. If you see an error instead, check that the add function and the print line are both in calculator.py and saved.
common_mistakes: Saving the file is missing: the terminal runs the file on disk, so press Cmd/Ctrl+S before running, or the print line will not be the version that runs.
Running from the wrong folder gives 'No such file or directory'. Use the terminal in the lesson folder.
Typing python calculator (no .py) or calculator.py alone. The file must be run with python calculator.py.
Indentation or a missing parenthesis in print(add(2, 3)) causes a SyntaxError. The line must match print(add(2, 3)) exactly, with two closing parentheses.

steps.title: Add three more operations
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, above the print line, write subtract, multiply and divide functions that each take a and b and return the result.

checks.label: subtract function is typed in the
multiply function is typed in the
divide function is typed in the

targets.caption: Leave the add function as it is, then type the three new functions below it, above the print line.

hints: Put each new function under add, with a blank line between them. The print line stays at the bottom.
Each function needs `def`, its name, `(a, b):`, and an indented `return` line. Indent the return by four spaces.
Subtract uses `a - b`, multiply uses `a * b`, and divide uses `a / b`. Don't worry about zero yet; that guard comes in step 4.
common_mistakes: Typing the new functions below the print line. They still work, but the terminal output comes before they're defined, so keep them above print.
Forgetting the colon after `(a, b)` or the indentation under `def`, which gives a SyntaxError when you run the file.
Writing `b - a` or `b / a` by mistake. Keep the first argument on the left so subtract(10, 4) returns 6.
Adding a zero check in divide now. That belongs to step 4, so keep divide to a single return line for this step.

steps.title: Guard against dividing by zero
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, make divide raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero") when b is 0 before returning a / b.

targets.caption: Type the new divide function on the line(s) below add

hints: Put divide below add, leaving one blank line between the two functions.
The guard is an if statement that checks whether b equals 0 before the division line runs.
Use two equal signs (==) for comparison; one (=) assigns a value and will cause an error.
common_mistakes: Writing `if b = 0:` with one equals sign, which is a syntax error.
Putting the `return a / b` line above the `if` check, so the division happens before the guard.
Forgetting the colon at the end of the `if` line or `def` line.
Indenting the `raise` or `return` lines inconsistently, so Python reports an IndentationError.
Misspelling the message so it no longer reads exactly "Cannot divide by zero".

steps.title: Read user input
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, replace the print line with a main() function that uses input() to read two numbers with float() and an operator symbol.
steps.code:
def main():
    first = float(input("First number: "))
    op = input("Operator (+, -, *, /): ")
    second = float(input("Second number: "))
    print(f"You entered {first} {op} {second}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

checks.label: main() function is in the editor
Calculator echoes the entered values in

precision_checks.label: calculator.py reads a number with float(input())

targets.caption: Type the new main() function below add()
Delete this print line; main() replaces it

hints: Delete the print(add(2, 3)) line first, then type main() in its place.
Each input() call pauses the program and waits for you to type in the terminal, then press Enter.
Wrap input() in float() for the two numbers so you can do math on them later; the operator stays a plain string.
common_mistakes: Leaving print(add(2, 3)) in the file, which runs before main() and clutters the output.
Forgetting the parentheses in def main(): or the colon at the end of the line.
Indenting the body of main() inconsistently; use four spaces for every line inside the function.
Dropping the if __name__ == "__main__": guard, so main() never runs when you execute the file.
Writing float(input(...)) without the closing parenthesis, which gives a SyntaxError.

steps.title: Pick the operation
steps.instructions: In main(), use if/elif on the operator (+, -, *, /) to call the matching function and print the result, with an else that prints Unknown operator.

checks.label: if/elif operator chain is in the
Unknown operator fallback is in the

precision_checks.label: module imports cleanly without running main

targets.match: # Step 1: Start building your calculator here
targets.caption: Type the main() function below this comment, after your add function

hints: Build main() one piece at a time: first read a, op, and b with input(), then add the if/elif chain.
Each condition compares op to a string in quotes, such as op == "+". Watch for the colon at the end of each if, elif, and else line.
Indent the body of every if, elif, and else by four spaces, and put the else's print under else:.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the quotes around the operator, so op == + is a syntax error instead of op == "+".
Using = instead of == in the comparisons, which raises a SyntaxError.
Missing the colon after elif or else, or mixing tabs and spaces in the indentation.
Calling subtract, multiply, or divide by names that differ from the functions you wrote in step 3 (check the def lines).
Running the script and typing an operator with extra spaces, such as ' +', which falls through to Unknown operator.

steps.title: Run the calculator
steps.instructions: At the bottom of calculator.py add if __name__ == "__main__": followed by an indented main() call.

checks.label: Code: main() is called under the

precision_checks.label: calculator.py calls main() indented under the

targets.caption: Go to the bottom of the file and type the main guard. Keep the main() line indented four spaces.

hints: Put the new lines at the very bottom of calculator.py, after everything else, with no indent on the if line.
The word after `__name__ ==` is the string "__main__" with two underscores on each side, and the colon at the end is required.
The main() line must be indented four spaces under the if, or Python will raise an IndentationError.
common_mistakes: Writing __name__ == main without quotes, or using __name__ = "__main__" with a single equals sign.
Forgetting the colon at the end of the if line.
Indenting the if line itself, or leaving main() unindented so it runs outside the guard.
Calling main() when no main function exists yet; if you have not defined main() in Step 6, define it first or Python will raise a NameError.
Running the file while it waits for input and leaving the terminal stuck; press Ctrl+C and type your answers when prompted.

steps.title: Try it in the terminal
steps.instructions: In the terminal, run python calculator.py and enter 8, 2 and / to see 4.0 printed.

targets.caption: Type this in the terminal, press Enter, then answer the prompts: 8, 2, and /

hints: Open the terminal in your lesson folder (the one with calculator.py) and run python calculator.py.
When it asks, type 8 and press Enter, then 2 and Enter, then / and Enter. Type only the value, no quotes.
If you see 4 instead of 4.0, convert your inputs with float(...) instead of int(...). On some systems use python3 calculator.py.
common_mistakes: Running the command from a different folder, giving 'No such file or directory'.
Typing all three values on one line (8 2 /) instead of pressing Enter after each.
Converting input with int() so the division logic or output differs from 4.0.
Typing the operation word 'divide' instead of the symbol / that your if/elif checks.
Forgetting to save calculator.py before running, so the old version runs.
